name: Dana Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm out of the Millbrook depot, which covers the hill country north of the river, mostly overhead lines on wooden poles. We're in the yard by seven, the foreman hands out the job sheets, and my crew of four loads the bucket truck and heads out. Most days it's swapping rotten poles, changing crossarms, hanging a new transformer for a farm that's added a cold store.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew, and I like the moment you close the switch and a whole valley gets its lights back. What wears me out is the call-outs, three in the morning in sleet, and then the pay slip, because Millbrook rates are well under what the city crews get for the same work. Since the company got sold to that investment fund, it's been overtime instead of hiring, and my knees know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That one I can believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say I told you so. The office people have been waving around these apps for two years and I still climb the same pole with the same hooks. Online I don't post much, but I'd probably share something from the union page about how the real problem was never robots, it was wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays as tight as it is now. We've got maybe two weeks of bills in the bank, and that's after Marco's bus-driving money. Nothing radical changing isn't the same as things being good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep going to the union meetings, because the contract is up next spring and Millbrook needs to close the gap with the city rates. I'd volunteer for the bargaining committee this time instead of just sitting at the back. Beyond that, same routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit flat, because relief doesn't pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the gap with the city rates. How big is it, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four an hour, last time we compared slips at the regional meeting. Over a year that's a car payment. Gus, who I eat lunch with in the truck, says he's been hearing "next contract" since before I was an apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about AI, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucia's twelve and she uses it for homework, which I don't love. I'd tell her it's a calculator with a big mouth. Learn to fix things, because the wind will always knock lines down and somebody has to go put them back.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so at work, because I still climb the same pole with the same hooks. Online I'd share the union line that the real problem was always wages, not robots.
S0.think: Privately she thinks nothing changing just means staying as tight as she is now, with about two weeks of bills saved. Nothing radical happening isn't the same as things being good.
S0.do: Keeps working her depot routine and joins the bargaining committee for next spring's contract instead of sitting at the back. Pushes to close the roughly four-an-hour gap with city crews.
S0.feel: Relieved, but flat, because relief doesn't pay the mortgage.
S0.quote: I'd tell her it's a calculator with a big mouth. Learn to fix things, because the wind will always knock lines down and somebody has to go put them back.
S0.fieldNote: Dana treats this picture as the default and turns straight to pay, which is what really occupies her. Her calm about AI sits on top of a constant money squeeze. The union is her main tool for change, and she is ready to step up in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's the one the managers would love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing at work and online: the machines don't climb, people do, and the company had better not use this as an excuse to cut crews. I'd be loud about that at the union meeting. Every change I've seen in eighteen years got sold as safety and turned out to be headcount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the patrol work goes first. Right now one of us drives the lines after a storm looking for damage, and a drone with one of these programs could do that faster. That's not my whole job, but it's the easy overtime, and the easy overtime is what keeps us afloat in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the extras right away. The kids' climbing club, the streaming, the second car insurance if Marco can share mine. I'd push the union to get it in writing that any drone or software work comes with retraining and no layoffs, and I'd wait and see what the company actually rolls out before doing anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's the feeling when the foreman says "we need to talk about the roster" and you know before he opens his mouth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn nothing new unless you had to. If the company offered a course on the drone software, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's paid time, yes, I'd sit in the room. I wouldn't go looking for it on my own phone at night. I'm not proud of that, but I've got enough on my plate between the kids and the call-outs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would get squeezed first if the overtime dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan, probably, because the bank on the main road is slower to chase than the mortgage people. Marco would hate that. Last time we were late he couldn't sleep for a week.

S1.say: She'd say loudly that machines don't climb, people do, and the company had better not use AI to cut crews. Every change she's seen in eighteen years got sold as safety and turned out to be headcount.
S1.think: She expects drones and software to take the storm patrol work first, which is the easy overtime that keeps the family afloat in winter. It's not her whole job, but it's the margin.
S1.do: Cuts the kids' climbing club, streaming and the second car insurance straight away. Pushes the union for written no-layoff and retraining terms, and waits to see what the company actually rolls out.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like when the foreman says he needs to talk about the roster.
S1.quote: Every change I've seen in eighteen years got sold as safety and turned out to be headcount.
S1.fieldNote: Her fear isn't losing the job but losing the overtime that bridges the gap in her pay. She'd take paid training but not learn on her own time, which she admits with some discomfort. She blames management choices rather than the technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union, the government, everybody, right now, because nobody's ready. Online I'd probably share every petition going. I'd be saying the grid is public infrastructure and it shouldn't be handed to a robot company because some fund wants a better quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared stiff. I'm average at this job, I'm not the one they keep for the tricky stuff, and there are maybe two other employers within an hour's drive who hire lineworkers. If robots can hang a transformer, a woman with a vocational certificate and two weeks of savings is the first one out the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Marco and the bank and see what we can stop paying. I'd cancel everything that isn't food, heat or the house. I'd be at every union meeting pushing for a fight over severance and job guarantees, and I'd be writing to our representative about income support, because there's no way families like ours get through this alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like standing at the bottom of a pole you can't see the top of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lucia and Tommy, that first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try not to scare them. I'd say Mum's work is changing and we're all going to be careful with money for a while. Tommy's nine, he'd ask if we're moving, and I honestly wouldn't know what to tell him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on the union and the government. What if neither moves fast enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know. My mother has a spare room two towns over, and that's the honest last resort. I'd rather fight for something than wait for it, but I can't fight for two years on two weeks of savings.

S2.say: She'd say the union and government need to act right now because nobody's ready, and share every petition. She'd argue the grid is public infrastructure and shouldn't be handed to robot firms for a fund's quarterly results.
S2.think: Privately she's scared stiff: she's average at the job, has a vocational certificate and two weeks of savings, and only two other lineworker employers within an hour. She expects to be first out the gate.
S2.do: Sits down with Marco and the bank in the first month and cancels everything except food, heat and the house. Attends every union meeting pushing for severance and job guarantees, and writes to her representative about income support.
S2.feel: Sick, like standing at the bottom of a pole she can't see the top of.
S2.quote: I'd rather fight for something than wait for it, but I can't fight for two years on two weeks of savings.
S2.fieldNote: This is where her thin savings and few local options collide. She still reaches for collective action and public support first, but admits her fallback is her mother's spare room. She is clear-eyed that being average makes her vulnerable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit of breathing room, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing as with the fast one, but I'd say it with a plan. Five years is one contract and a bit, so I'd be telling the crew this is the contract that matters. I'd want the union pushing for a law that says no robot work on live lines without a human crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years doesn't change where I end up, it changes how hard I land. I'm not going to become a programmer at 45. But five years is enough to clear the car loan and get a few months in the bank, if I'm strict.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting a fixed amount away every pay, even if it's small, maybe fifty a week, and pay the car off early. I'd put my name forward for union rep at Millbrook. And I'd sign every campaign for a fair transition, because a few years of warning means there's time to win something if enough of us push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. It's like a storm warning a day out instead of an hour out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not going to become a programmer. Is there anything you would learn, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the substation side, if the company paid for it. It's still hands-on but there's more switching and less climbing. My knees would thank me. But I'd want the union to make them pay for it, not me on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gus. He's fifty-eight, he's done thirty-five years, and he can't use a smartphone without swearing at it. If they push him out at sixty-one with nothing, that would break my heart. At least I've got some years left to scramble.

S3.say: She'd say the same thing as with the fast scenario but with a plan, telling the crew this is the contract that matters. She'd want the union pushing for a law requiring a human crew on live-line robot work.
S3.think: She thinks five years doesn't change where she ends up, only how hard she lands. It's enough time to clear the car loan and build a few months of savings if she's strict.
S3.do: Puts about fifty a week aside every pay and pays off the car loan early. Stands for union rep at Millbrook and backs campaigns for a fair transition, and would take substation training if the company paid.
S3.feel: Anxious but not frozen, like a storm warning a day out instead of an hour out.
S3.quote: Five years doesn't change where I end up, it changes how hard I land.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turns her fear into a savings plan and a bid to become union rep, but she still dreads the end point. She will only retrain on company time, which fits her resistance to new technology. Her worry for her older colleague Gus is strong and sincere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. My kids would be grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to do this properly, and if the company or the government wastes it, that's on them. I'd be saying it at work, at the school gate, everywhere. A decade is long enough to have a real plan for people like us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the first one where I can breathe a bit. Tommy would be nineteen. Lucia would be out of school. The mortgage would still be there, but the kids would be past the worst of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build up savings slowly and clear the car. I'd talk to Lucia properly about her studies, maybe push her towards nursing or something with people, not just a screen. I'd stay in the union and work on the transition clause, and I'd keep climbing, because a decade out I'd still be needed for most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still uneasy underneath, but it feels like something you can plan for instead of something that happens to you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You told me earlier you'd steer clear of new technology. With ten years, would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. If the union ran a course I'd go with the others. I'm stubborn, I know that. But I'm not stupid, and ten years is a long time to be stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your knees and your job at 53?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part I don't like thinking about. At 53 I'm too young for a pension and too old to start over. If the robots come then, I'd want a bridge, some kind of income until retirement age, and I'd be fighting for that from now.

S4.say: She'd say there's a decade to do this properly and if the company or government wastes it, that's on them. She'd say it at work, at the school gate and everywhere else.
S4.think: Privately ten years is the first picture where she can breathe, because the kids would be nearly grown. The mortgage would remain, but the family would be past the hardest stretch.
S4.do: Builds savings slowly, clears the car loan and talks with Lucia about studying for people-facing work like nursing. Stays active in the union on a transition clause and campaigns for an income bridge until pension age.
S4.feel: Still uneasy underneath, but it feels like something to plan for rather than something that happens to her.
S4.quote: I'm stubborn, I know that. But I'm not stupid, and ten years is a long time to be stubborn.
S4.fieldNote: Time matters to her mainly through her children's ages, not her own career. She shows a small crack in her resistance to new tools when the timeline is long. The gap she fears is 53 to pension age, and her answer is still political.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is a guarantee that nobody gets thrown off the crew without a bridge, real money until you find something or reach pension age, and paid retraining on company time. And honestly, a decent rate at Millbrook now, so I'm not starting from two weeks of savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. Not me, not the crew, not the people who keep the lights on. Some board in a city I've never been to will decide whether a robot climbs my pole, and nobody asks us.

headlineQuote: Some board in a city I've never been to will decide whether a robot climbs my pole, and nobody asks us.
portrait: Dana Rossi is a 43-year-old lineworker at a rural depot whose pay trails the city crews, with two school-age kids, a bus-driver partner and about two weeks of savings. She sees the union as her lever on everything, from wages now to severance later. In the mild pictures her worry is overtime and pay, not robots. The two-year AGI picture leaves her scared and reaching for petitions, cuts and her mother's spare room, while five and ten years turn that fear into savings plans and a run for union rep. She resists new technology but admits ten years is a long time to stay stubborn.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd be among the first out with two weeks of savings and few nearby employers.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income bridge until a new job or pension age, paid retraining on company time, and a fair rate at Millbrook now so she isn't starting from nothing.
